concept.name: Gambler's fallacy
aliases: Fallacy of the maturity of chances
concept.definition: The mistaken belief that, for independent random events, a run of one outcome makes the opposite outcome more likely next - as if chance had a memory and streaks must even out. Tversky and Kahneman traced it to the representativeness heuristic and the erroneous 'law of small numbers'.
concept.intuition: After five reds at roulette, black feels due - but the wheel has no memory and the odds are unchanged.
concept.mechanics: People expect short sequences to mirror long-run proportions, so they predict reversals after streaks in genuinely independent processes (negative recency). In trading it appears as expecting a rally purely because of a string of down days; it is the mirror image of the hot-hand fallacy.
concept.failure_modes: It is misapplied where events are actually dependent (cards drawn without replacement) or where a streak legitimately signals a biased process; inferring a loaded coin from twenty heads is Bayesian, not fallacious. In markets, streaks can reflect real regimes, which blurs the line between the fallacy and inference.
concept.misconceptions: Believing in long-run averages is not the fallacy; the fallacy is believing nature enforces them over the next few trials. Mean reversion in prices is a separate empirical claim, not a justification for the fallacy.
concept.example: A trader shorts an index after six consecutive up days, reasoning it is overdue for a down day, even though daily returns are close to independent and the streak carries no predictive information.
